intent: Changed: mass from 0.8 to 0.6 kg, with wheel_track reverted from 0.10 to 0.12 m. Kept the widened row (x = -0.024 to +0.024 m at y = 0.04 m), sensor_size 0.012 m, wheel radius, and body. Relative to the iteration 1 best (324.07), this is a single change (mass), so the race isolates the yaw-inertia hypothesis. Expected result: oval finish rate back near 0.7 and steering_oscillation at or below about 0.3, with s-bend and slalom max_error holding at or below about 0.064 m. Hypothesis A: lower yaw inertia reduces the turn-response lag that drives oscillation, so oscillation falls at the same yaw gain. Hypothesis B: lower mass gives less traction and more slip, so the oval finish rate does not recover. If B holds, the next candidate is a mass near 0.7 kg or a different controller-side gain, not a sensor change. I am considering a wheel_track near 0.11 m as a compromise if the oval recovers with mass alone, but I am not committing to it. I am not considering any further sensor-size or body changes.
learning: Iteration 3 showed that a shorter wheel track (higher yaw gain per unit control) hurt oval finishes and raised oscillation, so yaw gain is not the lever to pull. Iteration 4 tests whether mass, not track width, controls oscillation. Compare directly with iteration 1: same row, sensor size, and track, with only mass changed. If finishes recover and oscillation holds at or below about 0.3, mass is the useful lever. If finishes fall with higher oscillation, the lighter robot is losing traction or stability, and mass should move back toward 0.8 kg.
rationale: Iteration 3 changed only wheel_track (0.12 to 0.10 m) on the iteration 1 best design, and the score fell from 324.07 to 175.19. The oval finish rate dropped from 0.70 to 0.10, oval steering_oscillation rose from 0.26 to 0.33, and oval max_error stayed at about 0.064 m. The yaw-gain change therefore hurt the track that matters most for completions, so the shorter track is not the right fix. Slalom and s-bend did not gain enough to offset that loss. The Integrator's stated rule for this case is: if oscillation rises above about 0.3 with finishes falling, try mass 0.6 kg rather than further sensor or track changes. That condition is met on the oval, so I am following that advice. I am reverting wheel_track to 0.12 m, since the iteration 1 evidence shows that value gave the best oval result, and I am changing only mass (0.8 to 0.6 kg). This makes the candidate a single-variable test against the best raced design. Mass 0.6 kg lowers yaw inertia, which should shorten the turn-response lag that drives oscillation, and it keeps the sensor row and footprint that produced the oval gain. The Integrator's condition for keeping wheel_track 0.10 was not met, so I am not carrying it forward. I did not take the Integrator's earlier suggestion of a 0.016 m sensor, since iteration 2 showed that it collapsed the oval. I expect the oval finish rate to recover toward 0.7 with steering_oscillation at or below about 0.3. The risk is that lighter mass with an unchanged controller gain could raise oscillation instead, which would show up as falling finishes on the oval.
